opening.headline: Compare how Datadog, MLflow, Databricks, and Snowflake record the same LLM call with their own names and settings, and learn how to bundle cost and sensitive information into one system.
body: Imagine you are observing an LLM app with one team using Datadog, one team using MLflow, and a data team using Databricks and Snowflake. The same model call appears as a span somewhere and as a line of trace elsewhere. Even if you try to find the reason for the increase in costs, the same questions do not come with the same answers because each team uses different indicators and tags.

In this class, we will first look at Datadog's span types, transmission paths, indicators, and cost tags. Next, we check how MLflow traces are stored in Unity Catalog, Snowflake's observation function, and Databricks' budget, find common denominators among the four products, and organize them in a correspondence table. Lastly, we explain the problems of not being able to see the trace, the problem of sensitive information remaining, and the problem of tying the system together.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain differences in span, trace, and cost observation methods for each product
Explain why sensitive information protection and access control must be designed to overlap.

screens.title: Each product has different terminology and settings, resulting in different observation systems.
screens.lead: Open each item to see how observation systems diverge within an organization.

visual.alt: An illustration showing three teams using different observation products and the same LLM call recorded in different shapes for each product.

items.title: Same call, different name
items.body: An LLM call appears as a span in some products, and as a step or stored row within a trace in others. If the names are different, the conversation will be out of sync. Even if one team says the span was slow, the other team doesn't know what unit it is referring to. The starting point is to know what the calling units for each product are called.

items.title: There are different ways to find costs
items.body: If costs suddenly rise, you should first ask which model or app is responsible. However, each team sees different metrics and tags, so even if you ask the same question, you have to find the answer by model name in one place, credit usage history in another place, and budget screen in another place. If there is no standard, the total will not be correct.

items.title: Sensitive information remains in traces
items.body: A trace contains content such as input and output. If the prompt contains personal information or internal documents, it will be stored in the observation tool. This means that data collected for observation can become a new leak point, so no matter what product you use, you need to design both obscuration and access control together.

screens.outro: Rather than memorizing how to use products, this class is conducted by finding corresponding concepts between products.

screens.title: To recall: same call, different name.
screens.lead: Look at each question, think of your own answer first, and then select an item to see what you can think about. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a divergence in your observation system due to different terminology and settings for each product?
items.answer: If you have ever had a long meeting between teams using different tools and calling the same phenomenon under different names, the correspondence table in this class is the way to solve the problem. Matching names may seem trivial, but they are a prerequisite for discussing cost and quality.

items.prompt: When costs suddenly increased, were you able to immediately answer which model or app was responsible?
items.answer: You need to be able to break it down into model name, app name, and input and output tokens to get the answer. The topics of the screens that follow are whether these values ​​are recorded for each call, and whether custom tags can also be used for cost analysis.

items.prompt: Have you ever found out later that the trace still retains user input?
items.answer: Leaving observations on allows input and output to be saved. How to hide before saving, how to find and hide after saving, and how to limit who can see are different layers, and it is safe to overlap them.

screens.title: Datadog’s span types and measurement methods
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what kind of spans Datadog divides LLM calls into and which can be the root of the trace.

visual.alt: Trace structure with Retrieval, Embedding, LLM, and Tool span nested under the workflow root.

tabs.label: Types that can be a root
tabs.body: Datadog divides LLM call spans into types. Among them, LLM, Workflow, and Agent can be the root span of the trace. LLM means one model call, Workflow is a predetermined sequence of tasks, and Agent is a dynamic sequence in which the model decides what to do next. When a request comes in and starts with one of these, other types of spans are nested underneath it.

tabs.label: Types that cannot be root
tabs.body: Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval cannot be the root and are used as steps under spans such as Workflow or Agent. Tool is an external program or service call whose call arguments are created by LLM, Task is an independent step without an external service call, Embedding is a model or function call that creates an embedding, and Retrieval is a vector search step that retrieves a document from an external knowledge base. The documentation describes Embedding and Retrieval as subcategories of Tool, and you can see RAG behavior by writing the two spans together.

tabs.label: Workflow and Agent
tabs.body: Both types can be roots, but their meanings are different. Workflow is a task in which the code determines the order, and Agent changes the order as the model selects a tool. Even for the same app, the structure visible on the screen varies depending on the type of recording, so it is easier to interpret if it is selected according to the actual control method of the app.

tabs.label: Measurement method
tabs.body: Measurement can be done automatically or manually with the Agent Observability SDK, or by sending a span that follows the GenAI semantic convention of OpenTelemetry 1.37 or higher. The SDK supports Python (ddtrace), Node.js, and Java, while Go is experimental and only manual instrumentation is possible. The OpenTelemetry method can send API keys directly without SDK or Datadog Agent. Datadog documentation calls this product Agent Observability, and the document address and some materials use the name LLM Observability. Even though the names are different, the concepts of span and trace, which are recording units, are the same.

screens.outro: Once you have decided on the type, the subject of the next screen is where that data goes to arrive at Datadog.

screens.title: Agent and agentless: the path of data
screens.lead: Switch the toggles to compare the settings required and the path your data takes in both paths.

visual.alt: There are two paths from the app to Datadog: one that goes through the local agent and one that sends it directly.

states.label: Via Agent
states.body: In the path using Datadog Agent, the app's SDK sends data to the Agent, and the Agent delivers it to Datadog. In this case DD_API_KEY is not required. The documentation explains that API keys and agentless settings are only needed when not using an Agent. For your app, turn on the feature with DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED and give it a Datadog site (DD_SITE) and an app name (DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP). If you are already running an agent in an environment, the additional burden is small. Conversely, if the agent is not reached and agentless is not turned on, the trace will not arrive.

states.label: agentless
states.body: In agentless mode, the app sends data directly to Datadog without using Datadog Agent. In this case, DD_LLMOBS_AGENTLESS_ENABLED must be set to 1 or true, and DD_API_KEY and site (DD_SITE) must be set on the app side. Enable it by specifying DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1 and app name DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP. The app name is the standard for grouping traces and spans of the same app, and if not specified, the DD_SERVICE value is used. DD_LLMOBS_SAMPLE_RATE is the percentage of traces to keep, default is 1.0. When you don't see a trace, the first place to suspect is this path, key, and site.

screens.title: ml_obs metrics and cost_tags
screens.lead: Select an indicator row to see which questions each indicator is used for.

data.text:
ml_obs.span: number of spans  
ml_obs.span.duration: span duration  
ml_obs.span.error: Number of spans in error  
Token indicators: input, output, inference tokens  
Cache Metrics: Cache Reads, Cache Writes, Non-Cache Input Tokens  
Cost indicator: Cost estimated by number of tokens and supplier price (unit: nanodollars)

marks.span: ml_obs.span.error: Number of spans in error
marks.note: Error rate is the first question to narrow down which model or app is causing the call to fail. By dividing into model_name, model_provider, and ml_app tags, you can identify errors centered on a specific provider or app.

marks.span: Token indicators: input, output, inference tokens
marks.note: This is the answer to the question which model is more expensive. By dividing the input, output, and inference tokens, you can distinguish whether it is expensive because the prompt is long or because the answer is long.

marks.span: Cache Metrics: Cache Reads, Cache Writes, Non-Cache Input Tokens
marks.note: This is an indicator that the cache is actually having an effect. If the proportion of tokens read from the cache is low, it is a sign that configuring the cache to use it is not effective.

marks.span: Cost indicator: Cost estimated by number of tokens and supplier price (unit: nanodollars)
marks.note: The cost can be automatically estimated based on the number of tokens in the span and the unit price disclosed by the provider, or you can enter the value directly. When entering directly, it is specified in dollars and stored as nanodollars. The custom tag attached to the span must be keyed to cost_tags (costTags in Node.js) to become a tag for the cost/token indicator. Use it for tags with limited value types, such as team or feature, and avoid values ​​such as user ID.

Used to determine what type of span is causing the delay. By dividing by span_kind tag, you can distinguish whether model call or search is slow. However, custom tags defined by cost_tags are not applied to this metric.

screens.outro: These metrics are calculated based on 100% traffic. Tags that can be used in span indicators (ml_obs.span series) are env, error, ml_app, model_name, model_provider, service, span_kind, and version, and other tags attached to span are not provided as indicator tags.

screens.title: Saving MLflow tracing and Unity Catalog traces
screens.lead: Compare the two storage methods in the table and think about which question is right for you.

data.caption: Two ways to store MLflow traces
rows: Search with MLflow UI and Python SDK
In addition to UI and SDK, we analyze with SQL, Genie Code, AI/BI dashboard, and Spark-based tools.
There is a limit of 100,000 traces per experiment
Manage Unity Catalog schema and table permissions
Saved in OTel format, making it compatible with other OpenTelemetry clients
This is an alternative repository used when there is no Unity Catalog trace location.
When creating an experiment, the trace location is specified and connected using catalog, schema, and table_prefix, and cannot be changed to a different location afterward.
For trace tables, ALL_PRIVILEGES is not enough; MODIFY and SELECT must be explicitly granted.
data.notes: Databricks recommends storing Unity Catalog for new and production workloads. When you turn on MLflow automatic logging, a trace with a step-by-step span is created for each agent execution, and the experiment becomes the entry point to the UI, regardless of which repository you use. Since connections can only be made when creating an experiment, it is a good idea to choose a storage method first.

screens.title: Snowflake AI Observability and Cost Observation
screens.lead: Hover over or select a highlighted term to see what that feature observes and where it looks.

data.text: In Snowflake, the observation targets vary by feature. Cortex Agents provides real-time threads and traces along with batch evaluation. CoCo accumulates prompt traces into event table and retrieves credits and tokens from Account Usage. When REQUEST_LOGGING is enabled, requests are logged into Cortex Search, and custom-built applications are observed via TruLens. Built-in functions such as AI_COMPLETE do not record traces but are only verified through Account Usage. Expenses are monitored via Budgets and Notifications, with totals evaluated based on Account Usage.

terms.tip: It shows real-time threads and traces, and also provides batch evaluation of the dataset.

Traces from Cortex Agents, CoCo, Cortex Search, and TruLens are stacked in SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS. Delivery is on a best effort basis, so totaling costs using this table may result in less than the actual cost.
This is where you can view usage history such as credits, tokens, models, and request IDs for each AI function, and use it as the basis for cost reporting.
If REQUEST_LOGGING is turned on, one row is accumulated for each request, and the agent_type is specified as CORTEX SEARCH SERVICE in GET_AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS to search.
This tool is used to send traces and evaluations of custom AI applications you create, whether hosted inside or outside of Snowflake, to your Snowflake account for observation.

Snowflake Budgets sets a monthly credit limit for an account or set of objects and sends you notifications when the limit is expected to be exceeded. Evaluation occurs periodically, not instantaneously.

screens.title: What the same call looks like in your product
screens.lead: Move the slider to change products and compare what the same concept corresponds to in each product.

stops.body: The calling unit is LLM span. Cost is viewed as the ml_obs cost indicator, apps are grouped with the ml_app tag, and access control is controlled using this tag and RBAC. Data is stored in the Datadog service.

The calling unit is a span within a trace. The storage is the Delta table in Unity Catalog and the access control is schema and table permissions. Because it is in OpenTelemetry format, it is portable.

A call unit is a span recording of a trace and is stacked in the AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS event table. Costs are searched using Account Usage tokens and credits, and the event table is not used as a basis for cost totals as it is a best effort delivery.

Databricks budgets are in USD and calculated from the product's list price. Track spending across your account, workspace, or custom tag ranges and send email reminders when you hit monthly thresholds. Since it looks at spending units rather than call units and is not suitable to be used as an absolute spending cap, call-level costs should be read together with the token information in the trace.

The common features of the four products are span, token, model name, and error. By organizing around these common fields, you can answer the same questions in the same way, even for different products.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Search order when traces are not visible and costs are rising
screens.lead: Follow the example and open the steps one by one to see which settings are checked and in what order.

steps.title: sorting out the situation
steps.body: Traces for newly deployed services are not visible in Datadog, and monthly costs for other existing services have suddenly increased. The two issues are separate. The former is a problem of data not arriving, and the latter is a problem of how to divide and read the data that has arrived. If you mix them together, it will take longer to find the cause, so check them separately.

steps.title: Check transfer settings
steps.body: Missing traces check in that order: whether instrumentation is turned on (DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED), whether the transmission path is via agent or agentless, whether the key and site are correct, and whether the app name (ml_app) is the expected value. If you do not use Agent, data will not arrive if agentless settings, API key, and site are not present on the app side.

steps.title: Sampling confirmation
steps.body: If the settings are correct but only part of the trace is visible, check whether the sampling rate (DD_LLMOBS_SAMPLE_RATE) or sampling rule is truncating the trace. However, the ml_obs metric is calculated based on 100% traffic, so even if you see only a small trace, the metric reflects all calls. Knowing this difference can help you distinguish between what is invisible due to sampling and what is truly not being transmitted.

steps.title: Split the cost
steps.body: For cost increase, we break down input, output, and cache token metrics by model name and app. You can see the direction of increase by checking whether the output tokens of a specific model have increased or the cache read rate has decreased.

steps.title: Break it down further with tags
steps.body: If you want to divide by team or function, the custom tag attached to the span must be keyed in cost_tags (costTags in Node.js). If not specified, the tag cannot be used in the cost/token indicator even though it is in the span. Choose only tags with limited values, such as team or customer ratings, and avoid tags with infinite values, such as user ID or request ID, as they may be truncated or omitted from the metrics.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Problem with sensitive information remaining in traces
screens.lead: Open the case's protections layer by layer to see what risks are being reduced and where.

visual.alt: Illustration of four layers of protection on the way from app to storage.

items.title: situation
items.body: Let's assume a consultation chatbot. This chatbot's prompts and responses, including your social security number and account number, are stored in Trace. The user entered the information for consultation and did not intend to leave it in the observation tool. The problem is that once saved, anyone who can view the trace will see these values.

items.title: 1st layer: Hide in the app layer
items.body: With the span processor of the Agent Observability SDK, you can mask the input and output of a span depending on conditions, or prevent the span itself from being exported. This is the earliest possible protection, as the app processes it before sending it to Datadog. It can be selectively applied based on conditions such as tags.

items.title: 2nd layer: Find and cover up what’s left
items.body: Sensitive Data Scanner identifies and masks sensitive information that may remain, such as personal information, financial information, and internal information. Its role is to filter out values ​​missed by the app-level rules.

items.title: Layer 3: Access Control
items.body: Since there may be information that is not covered, the viewing range is also limited. By using Datadog's Data Access Control on the ml_app tag, you can restrict the teams and roles that can view traces for that app. When using OpenTelemetry measurements, some data may be recorded in APM traces, so consider configuring Restricted Dataset for APM as well.

items.title: Layer 4: Storage Permissions
items.body: If traces are saved in Unity Catalog, viewing is restricted by the trace table's schema and table permissions. The key is to overlap so that even if one layer is punctured, the next layer will block it.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Binding split systems into common fields
screens.lead: Toggle the toggle to compare how your team's metric names change before and after mapping.

states.label: Before mapping
states.body: The Datadog team calls the same information by ml_app and model_name tags, the MLflow team calls it trace properties, and the Snowflake team calls it the Model and Token columns in Account Usage. Every time we create an expense report, our team has to manually transcribe names and independently check that the totals are correct. It is not determined which team's value is the standard.

states.label: After mapping
states.body: First, define common fields. Starting points include the app name, model name, provider, input token, output token, and whether there are any errors. Next, create a table that maps tags and column names for each product to this field. Where exports can be made in OpenTelemetry format, the format is unified to ensure portability. By using one cost dashboard as a baseline and comparing the rest against this table, you can quickly find where the totals are off.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the content covered in this class in one place.

paragraphs: Datadog divides spans into LLM, Workflow, Agent, Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval, and only the first three can be the root of the trace. Data is sent through a local Agent or directly agentless. In agentless, the API key and site are required on the app side, and if you don't see the trace, check this path setting first.

The ml_obs metric shows span count, duration, errors, tokens, cache tokens, and cost based on 100% traffic. Costs can be estimated by the number of tokens and supplier price, or entered directly. If you want to split costs and tokens with custom tags, you must specify a key in cost_tags.

MLflow traces can be saved in the Unity Catalog in OpenTelemetry format, analyzed with SQL, and controlled with table permissions. Snowflake tracks your spending with Cortex feature traces and Account Usage, while Databricks tracks your spending with budgets and alerts.

Sensitive information is not blocked by a single device. It is layered by blocking it at the app level with a span processor, finding remaining values ​​with a scanner, and restricting viewing with access control and storage permissions. Even if the products are different, the system can be tailored with common fields such as span, token, model name, and error.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Although each product has a different name, the span, token, model, and error are common. Design costs and protection based on these common fields.

screens.title: Reflecting on Concept Cards
screens.lead: Select a card, turn it over, and summarize the key concepts one more time.

cards.back: This is the kind of work span did in Datadog. LLM, Workflow, and Agent can be the root of a trace, but Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval cannot. Even within the same app, the screen structure varies depending on the type of recording.

This is a mode where the app sends data directly to Datadog without using Datadog Agent. Specifies when not using Agent, and API key and site settings are required on the app side. If you can't see the trace, check this setting first.

This parameter specifies the key to be passed to the cost/token indicator among the user-defined tags attached to the span. In Node.js, it's costTags. If not specified, the tag will not be used to divide the cost even though it is in the span.

This method saves MLflow traces in the Delta table in OpenTelemetry format. There is no limit to the number of experiments per experiment, analysis is performed using SQL, and access is controlled using schema and table permissions. MODIFY and SELECT must be explicitly granted.

It is designed to block sensitive information by dividing it into multiple layers of span processor, sensitive data scanner, access control, and storage permissions. This is a structure in which the values ​​missed by one device are filtered out by the next device.

misconceptions.myth: The span type is the same for each product.
misconceptions.fact: Since the name and scope are different for each product, a correspondence table is necessary.

misconceptions.myth: The tag attached to the span automatically becomes the tag of the cost indicator.
misconceptions.fact: You must specify a key as cost_tags to use it as a tag for cost indicators.

misconceptions.myth: If the traces are centered, there is no need for access control.
misconceptions.fact: Since sensitive information is gathered in one place, permissions and screening are essential.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Knowing the span type and measurement method allows for correspondence between products.
The data path is different between agent-based and agentless, and the inspection items are also different.
Costs are decomposed into ml_obs indicators and cost_tags, and traces saved in Unity Catalog are analyzed using SQL.
Sensitive information is covered in multiple layers and access is restricted.
